title: Erectile Dysfunction among Male University Students in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Prevalence, Associated Factors, and Help-Seeking
content: Background: Data on erectile dysfunction (ED) in young African men are scarce. We estimated ED prevalence among male university students in Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso, and examined associated factors, psychosocial impact, and help-seeking. Methods: In this cross-sectional online survey (January-July 2026), male students aged 18-30 years at Joseph Ki-Zerbo University completed an anonymous questionnaire. The five-item International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) was scored in men who had attempted intercourse in the previous four weeks, with ED defined as a score of 21 or less. Associated factors were examined by multivariable logistic regression. Results: Of 696 respondents (mean age 24.1 ± 3.2 years), 476 were evaluable. ED was present in 240 (50.4%; 95% CI 45.9-54.9); it was mild in 151 and moderate or severe in 20. Self-reported depression (adjusted odds ratio 4.04; 95% CI 1.10-14.88) and other chronic conditions (1.87; 1.11-3.15) were independently associated with ED; age, alcohol, and tobacco use were not. Among men with ED, 66.5% reported interference with academic work, and only 11.9% of those acknowledging a problem had consulted a health professional. Shame was the most cited barrier (61.4%). Conclusions: Mostly mild ED was common in this sample and was linked to depression and chronic illness rather than lifestyle. Campus services should offer confidential sexual and mental health screening.
